summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing British Overseas Territory with its own Parliament and its own Supreme Court, which between them make and interpret its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council, and no such extension appears in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap facing a trans visitor is gender recognition. No process exists in Gibraltar for changing a legal gender marker, and the sourced material records that transgender persons are not permitted to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore travels on a document whose marker cannot be altered by any local route, and can expect to be read at the border and in public under that marker.

Statutory discrimination protection covering gender reassignment, alongside sexual orientation, has been in place since 2007 under Gibraltar's own equality provisions.

Hate-crime coverage now extends to trans people. Parliament amended the Crimes Act in September 2013 to criminalise hatred and harassment on grounds of sexual orientation, with royal assent on 25 September and effect from 10 October 2013, and in July 2026 passed a bill amending hate crime and hate speech legislation to include protections for transgender identity.

In July 2026 Parliament also passed a bill making it an offence to offer or practise conversion therapy.

Partner and family recognition is established locally: civil partnerships since 2014, same-sex marriage since December 2016 after a bill passed unanimously, a Supreme Court ruling of 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution, and an Adoption Act 2023 in full effect from 18 April 2024 that expressly allows same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

The age of consent for all sexual activity regardless of sexuality or gender is 16. The Supreme Court ruled on 8 April 2011 that the previous age of 18 for gay sex was unconstitutional, and the gender-neutral Crimes Act 2011, approved in August 2011, set the equal age of 16 with effect from 23 November 2012.

The House of Commons Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 inquiry into overseas territories recommended that discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender status be made illegal in all overseas territories, and its Seventh Report of 2007-08 sets accountability and good-governance expectations applicable to Gibraltar.
tangentialFactors:
Gibraltar's framework diverges from United Kingdom law on two points that matter to a trans visitor. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 does not extend to Gibraltar of its own force, and the United Kingdom's 2025 code on single-sex services, which governs access to women-only spaces in the parent jurisdiction, binds Gibraltar only through an Order in Council that the sourced material does not record.

Official response to anti-LGB abuse has been rhetorical and investigative rather than adjudicated. In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would urgently consider legislation against what the Chief Minister called disgusting lurking homophobia on social media during Pride month, and the Ministry began examining a proposal to make denigration on the basis of sexual orientation a specific criminal offence.

The trajectory of Gibraltar's own legislation runs toward wider coverage: sexual-orientation hate crime in 2013, transgender identity added to hate crime and hate speech in July 2026, and conversion therapy criminalised in the same month. No enforcement data accompanies any of these measures in the sourced material.

External oversight has been limited to recommendations. The Foreign Affairs Committee's 2008 inquiry urged that sexual orientation or gender status discrimination be outlawed across overseas territories; the Committee's Seventh Report of 2007-08 frames accountability and good-governance expectations rather than binding obligations.
localsOnly:
Family law is settled for residents. The Supreme Court of Gibraltar held on 10 April 2013 that section 5(2) of the Adoption Act 1951 violated the Gibraltar Constitution after a long-term lesbian couple denied adoption challenged the law, and Parliament amended the position through the 2014 civil partnership legislation. The Adoption Act 2023 took full effect on 18 April 2024 and explicitly allows same-sex couples to adopt without discrimination.

Reproductive assistance is available locally on stated terms. In February 2021 Gibraltar enacted a surrogacy law permitting non-commercial, altruistic surrogacy for married couples or civil partners unable to conceive, with automatic recognition of children of same-sex couples conceived through artificial insemination, and in June 2017 the Gibraltar Health Authority approved an amendment to its in vitro fertilisation policy allowing lesbian couples to access assisted reproductive technology.

Same-sex marriage was legislated after a December 2015 consultation that left Gibraltarians polarised; a government minister presided over an inter-ministerial committee weighing the viewpoints, and the amending bill for the Civil Marriage Act went to Parliament in August 2016 before passing unanimously in December 2016.

Sexual activity between men was legalised in 1993. Before the 2011 reforms, gay male minors faced a discriminatory age of 18, and a private member's bill to equalise consent was defeated in Parliament on 18 May 2009.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the bills Parliament passed in July 2026 on transgender-identity hate protections and on conversion therapy received royal assent, and the dates on which they take effect, are not stated in the sourced material.

No source addresses how Gibraltar immigration or border officers handle a passport whose gender marker does not match the holder's presentation, nor whether any secondary screening, referral or medical examination procedure applies to trans arrivals.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare in Gibraltar, whether treatment prescribed abroad is dispensed locally, and any waiting-list or referral requirement are not sourced here.

Facilities law, including which toilets or changing rooms a trans person may use, has no entry in the sourced inventory, and the effect of the United Kingdom's 2025 single-sex-services code in Gibraltar without an Order in Council extension is unresolved beyond the fact that no extension appears.

Enforcement record for the 2013 sexual-orientation hate-crime provision and for the 2007 discrimination protections is not documented, including any prosecutions, complaints outcomes or damages awarded.
